title: 1-D convolution: padding, stride and output size
subtitle: Slide a small kernel along a signal and see where o = ⌊(i + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1 comes from.

intro.idea: A convolutional layer slides a short kernel of k weights along an input of length i. At each position it multiplies the overlapping numbers and adds them up, giving one output value. Padding p adds zeros at both ends, and the stride s is how far the kernel jumps between positions.
intro.why: The output length o decides the shape of every later layer in a CNN. Getting it wrong is one of the most common bugs when designing networks, and padding/stride are the knobs that control it.
steps: Pad the input with p zeros on each side, giving length i + 2p.
Place the kernel at the left end; multiply element-wise with the input under it and sum. That is output y<sub>1</sub>.
Move the kernel s steps to the right and repeat, as long as it still fits inside the padded input.
The number of positions that fit is o = ⌊(i + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1.

explorations.title: Padding changes the output length
explorations.change: Press Try it (i = 5, k = 3, valid). Then switch the padding to half/same and to full.
explorations.observe: o goes 3 → 5 → 7. With half padding the output has the same length as the input; with full padding every partial overlap is counted.
explorations.why: With p zeros on each side the kernel can start at i + 2p − k + 1 positions. p = 0 gives 3, p = 1 gives 5, p = 2 gives 7.

explorations.title: “Convolution” in CNNs does not flip the kernel
explorations.change: Press Try it (an impulse input), then turn on Flip the kernel.
explorations.observe: Without flipping the output is (3, 2, 1), the kernel read backwards. With flipping it is (1, 2, 3), a copy of the kernel.
explorations.why: Deep-learning libraries compute cross-correlation and still call it convolution. Textbook (signal-processing) convolution flips the kernel first. For learned kernels this does not matter, since the network can learn the flipped weights, but it matters when you compare with hand-designed filters.

limitations: One channel, one kernel, no bias and no non-linearity. Real convolutional layers sum over many input channels and use many kernels.
Only 1-D inputs; the same output-size formula applies independently along each axis of a 2-D image.
Half padding p = ⌊k/2⌋ keeps o = i only for odd k and s = 1.
The floor in the formula means some input values at the right end can be skipped when the stride does not divide evenly.

tests.name: Valid, i=5 k=3 s=1 gives o=3

source.paper: A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep learning

supported.claim: With no padding and unit stride the output size is o = (i − k) + 1.
Half padding keeps the output size equal to the input size (odd k, s = 1).
Full padding gives o = i + k − 1.

simplifications: The paper works with 2-D inputs; we use a single 1-D axis because the relationships apply per axis.
The impulse and edge-detector examples and the flip toggle are our own illustrations.
